## Life Summary

Alan Dale Telfer was born on 27 October 1890 in Tantanoola, South Australia, the 13th child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge.

He never married. During the Great Depression of the 1920s-1930s, Alan migrated far from the agricultural safety of South Australia's Limestone Coast to the interior of New South Wales. He found work as a **ganger** (railway labor foreman) and **coalminer** — a gruelling and highly itinerant profession that took him deep into the state's central-west.

### Death — Resolved (NSW Government Gazette)

Alan's fate was a long-standing mystery in the Telfer family tree. The resolution came via an NSW Government Gazette intestate estate notice, which confirmed:

> Alan Dale Telfer, late of **Wilga Tank, Girilambone**, in the State of New South Wales, died **intestate** on **13 September 1937**.

Girilambone and the associated Wilga Tank area was a remote railway siding and copper mining outpost in central-western New South Wales. His death there, without a will, paints a picture of a rugged, transient, and likely impoverished life in his final years — a stark contrast to the settled farming life of his Tantanoola siblings.

His exact burial location is unknown but likely in the Girilambone district.

| 13 Nov 1921 | Mother Martha Clara Henstridge died at Adelaide |
| 13 Sep 1937 | Died intestate at Wilga Tank, Girilambone, NSW |

## Life Summary

Alma Ida Sporer was born in about 1881, likely in the Mount Gambier / Kongorong district of South Australia. Her surname appears in records as Sporer (most common), Spehr (original German spelling), and Spörer — typical of German Lutheran families in South Australia's south-east.

On 24 October 1917, at the age of 37, she married James Telfer (aged 49) at the Lutheran Church in Mount Gambier. The marriage was announced in the *Border Watch* on 26 October 1917. Their only child, Vida, was born on 8 March 1919 at Glencoe West.

Alma outlived James by nearly 19 years. She died on 23 April 1965 at Felixstow (a suburb of Adelaide), aged 83–84. Her Last Residence was recorded as Felixstow. She was buried in Lake Terrace Cemetery, Mount Gambier, Section K, Plot 379.

The Sporer family has roots in the Kongorong district south of Mount Gambier, with several Sporer burials at Lake Terrace Cemetery.

## Life Story

Caroline Amelia Masters was born on **10 June 1842** in the village of **Tiffield, Northamptonshire, England**. She was just three years old when her family emigrated to South Australia aboard the **Templar**, arriving at Port Adelaide on **24 November 1845**.

Her father **Charles Masters** (1809–1866) was a farmer who established "Wroxton Grange" near Angaston, South Australia, and was a noted horse breeder. He died in 1866 of liver complications and was buried at Angaston Old Cemetery.

On **22 September 1874**, Caroline married **John Telfer** at the Baptist Chapel, Tarlee. Together they raised **six sons** at Willow Plains, near Clare, where they lived for 47 years.

### The Tragic Conclusion

In a remarkable and poignant end to a long marriage, Caroline died **within hours** of her husband John in August 1929. John passed away on **23 August 1929**, and Caroline followed him the next day, **24 August 1929**. The *Register News-Pictorial* (Adelaide) ran a photograph captioned:

> "THE LATE MRS. JOHN TELFER, of Clare, who died within a few hours of her husband. Both were prominent Clare residents."

They are buried together at **Clare Cemetery, South Australia**.

- Thomas Hosking (1821–1854) and Catherine May (1817–1908) immigrated to South Australia in **1847**
- Ship: Not yet confirmed. Searched "La Belle Alliance" (arr. 2 Jul 1847) — no Hosking listed on WikiTree passenger profiles. Searched "Santipore" (arr. 1848) — a Facebook post mentions a different Thomas Hosking arriving on this ship in 1848.

## Life Summary

David Parker was born in **Tarbolton, Ayrshire, Scotland** in 1822, son of Hugh Parker and Christian Fulton. He worked as a **victualler** (licensed victualler/innkeeper) in the St Quivox area of Ayrshire — the 1851 census shows him at Wallace Street, Wallacetown, with wife Isabella, infant son William H, and a servant.

### Immigration

In 1852, David made the life-changing decision to emigrate to South Australia. He sailed from Liverpool aboard the barque **Martin Luther**, arriving in Adelaide on **4 May 1852** with his wife Isabella and three children.

### Life in Australia

The family pioneered in the **Port Gawler / Virginia / Peachy Belt** districts north of Adelaide. David's first wife Isabella died in 1867, and he remarried to Clementina Minto in Adelaide in 1871.

He moved north to the **Port Pirie** area later in life, establishing "Wheatlands" farm. He died there on 4 April 1888, aged 65, described as "respected by all who knew him."

## Life Summary

Elizabeth Beattie Telfer was born in Kelso, Roxburghshire, Scottish Borders, Scotland, likely around 1832–1834, the daughter of James Telfer (1796–1863) and Elizabeth Beattie (1802–1891). She grew up in the rural Scottish borderlands, a region known for sheep farming and textile weaving.

In 1854, at approximately age 20–22, Elizabeth immigrated to Australia on the ship *Oliver Lang* with her brothers James and Robert. The ship landed in Melbourne, and the siblings travelled overland to South Australia, where they visited her uncle Francis Telfer at "Macoota," Kersbrook.

On **18 December 1856**, Elizabeth married **John Charles Dillon** at the residence of Francis Telfer, Chain of Ponds, South Australia. The marriage was registered at Talunga, SA, Volume 8, Page 376.

Between 1858 and 1871, Elizabeth bore nine children at their home in the Para Wirra / Chain of Ponds district. The family was deeply connected to the Mount Lofty Ranges — John Charles Dillon acquired land sections 648, 5517, and 5521 in the Hundred of Para Wirra in 1860 under the new Torrens Title system.

Elizabeth passed away on 17 February 1896 in Norwood, SA (age 62), and was buried at Houghton Cemetery. Her husband John survived her by a decade, dying in 1906 at Tea Tree Gully.

# Francis Telfer (~1809–1895)

**Role:** Scottish immigrant — founder of the Australian Telfer line
**Also known as:** Francis Telfer of Blackburnfoot

**Died:** 2 September 1895 (aged 86) — Hope Farm, Tarlee, South Australia

**Arrival:** *Prince George* — London 12 Sep 1838 → Port Adelaide 26 Dec 1838 (105 days)
**Occupation:** Farmer and storekeeper — Macoota, Chain of Ponds, Kersbrook
**Religion:** Baptist Church — principal supporter at Kersbrook
**Great-great-grandson:** [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]]
**Brother (Scotland):** [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] — married Elizabeth Beattie, stayed in Scotland
**Great-great-great-grandson:** [[Mark Telfer (1877–1946)]]

---

## Family

| **Father** | James Telfer (1761–1845) — see Research section |

| **Children** | James Telfer (b. 1832 Scotland), Esther Jane Smith (1834), Elizabeth Farrow (1836), Jane Telfer (1840), [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]], George Wright Telfer, Margaret Dougal Telfer |

---

## Life Story

### Scottish Roots

Francis Telfer was born on **2 February 1809** at **Blackburnfoot**, in the parish of Castleton, Roxburghshire, in the Scottish Borders — a rugged, rolling landscape of sheep farms and river valleys. He began his married life at Langshawburn, Dumfriesshire, working the land as his forebears had done for generations.

His first child, James, was baptised on **3 March 1832** in Scotland.

### The Voyage — Prince George, 1838

The Telfer family joined the wave of assisted immigration to South Australia, sailing from London on **12 September 1838** aboard the **Prince George** — a 482-ton barque built in Bristol. She was a workhorse ship, previously used for convict transport (250 convicts to NSW in 1837).

On board were **199 passengers** (126 adults, 73 children). The 105-day voyage took them across the Atlantic, around the Cape of Good Hope, and across the Southern Ocean. They arrived at **Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838**.

### New Life in South Australia

After a short stay near Magill, Francis settled at **Kersbrook, in the Chain of Ponds district** of the Adelaide Hills. He farmed the land, opened a store, and became a pillar of the local **Baptist Church**, serving as its principal supporter for many years.

### Three Marriages

Francis married **three times** in his long life:

1. **Jean (Jane) Murray** — married in Scotland. She died and was buried on **22 January 1839**, only weeks after arriving in the colony. Mother of his first three children.
2. **Dinah Flavel** — his second wife in the colony.
3. **Margaret Wright** — his third wife, and mother of [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] and the younger children.

### Final Years

After his wife Margaret died, Francis's health declined. He moved in with his son **G. W. Telfer** at Gawler, then spent his last four months at **Hope Farm, Tarlee**, with his daughter **Mrs. Farrow**.

He passed away on **2 September 1895** at age 86 and was buried at **Tarlee Cemetery**. At his graveside were three fellow passengers from the *Prince George* — "namely, his daughter (Mrs. Farrow), Mr. Thos. Flavel, and Mr. W. Flavel, of Kapunda" — testament to the bonds formed on that voyage 57 years earlier.

### The Prince George

No known painting or drawing of the actual *Prince George* (1830 Bristol barque) survives. The closest visual reference available — **"The Barque J.P. Smith" by Samuel Walters, 1840** — is a portrait of a near-identical barque painted just two years after the Telfer family's voyage, by the premier British merchant ship portraitist of the era.

**Source:** National Maritime Museum, Greenwich, London (BHC3432). Public domain.  
[View on RMG Collections](https://www.rmg.co.uk/collections/objects/rmgc-object-14905)

> **Ship details:** The *Prince George* was a 482-ton wooden barque built in Bristol in 1830. She carried Francis Telfer and 198 other passengers from London to Port Adelaide in 105 days (12 Sep — 26 Dec 1838). This reference ship — the *J.P. Smith* — was the same rig type (three-masted barque), similar tonnage, and painted in the same decade by Samuel Walters, the most celebrated painter of British merchant ships in the 1840s.

## Obituary (from contemporary newspaper)

> **DEATH OF AN OLD COLONIST.** An old South Australian resident, Mr. Francis Telfer, died at Hope Farm, Tarlee, on Monday, 2nd inst. He was born at Black Burn fort, Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland, in 1809, and arrived in South Australia by the Prince Alfred in 1838. After a short residence near Magill he settled at Kersbrook, Chain of Ponds, and carried on farming there until the death of his wife some three years ago... The deceased leaves two sons — Mr. John Telfer, of Hawker, and Mr. G. W. Telfer, Willaston — and three daughters — Mrs. Farrow, of Hope Farm, Mrs. Smith, of Canouba, New South Wales, and Mrs. A. F. Telfer, of Edgerston, Tantanoola. ... The late Mr. Telfer was a good Christian, a member of the Baptist Church, and for many years was its principal supporter at Kersbrook.

**Verdict: STRONG SECONDARY EVIDENCE — Parents accepted for family tree.**

**Verification Method:** Independent cross-reference of all sources cited by The Librarian, plus direct inspection of FindAGrave and WikiTree pages via browser (bypassing Cloudflare blocks).

**Confirmed Evidence:**

1. **Statutory Death Index Scotland (PRIMARY SOURCE)** — WikiTree Telfer-949 (William Telfer 1811-1888) cites the Statutory Death Index: "Edinburgh St George 1888 685/1 888 Age 77 Mother's maiden surname **Hutton**." This is a genuine primary source — Scottish statutory death records entered the mother's maiden name, something parish records sometimes omit. William's mother being Betty Hutton directly connects the family unit.

2. **FindAGrave Memorial 170769918 (James Telfer)** — Verified via browser. The descriptive text explicitly says "James and Betty (Hutton) Telfer had children" and lists Francis Telfer 1809-1895 as child #7 of 8. Caveat: Francis is listed in the body text but NOT in the formal "Family Members" section (which only links 5 of the 8 children who have their own memorial pages).

3. **WikiTree Telfer-949 (William Telfer)** — Biography states "son of James telfer and Betty Hutton." Cites Family Search and Scottish Church Registers as additional sources beyond the Statutory Death Index.

4. **Geographic Consistency** — Both Blackburnfoot (Francis's birthplace per headstone) and Sorbietrees (James Telfer's farm) are in Castleton parish, Roxburghshire (Liddesdale), approximately 4 miles apart.

5. **"Francis Hutton Telfer"** — Ancestry records show the middle name "Hutton," consistent with the Scottish naming practice of using the mother's maiden surname as a middle name.

**Conflation Warning** — WikiTree Telfer-400 (Francis Telfer) contains a DATA ERROR in the structured fields: it lists death location as "Taree, New South Wales" instead of "Tarlee, South Australia." The biography text (quoting the actual Border Watch death notice) correctly says Tarlee. This is an entry error in the WikiTree data fields (possibly an autocorrect confusion) and does NOT invalidate the profile — our vault has the correct information.

**Gold-Standard Gap** — No OPR (Old Parish Register) baptismal entry was directly consulted. The Castleton OPRs (1697-1819) are on microfilm at ScotlandsPeople and FamilySearch but were not accessed. An OPR baptismal record for Francis would be the definitive proof. The existing evidence is strong but converging — all sources point in the same direction without contradiction.

**⚠️ Update 5 Jun 2026:** While Francis's OPR baptism remains unconfirmed, his **father James Telfer's OPR baptism has now been identified** via FamilySearch IGI batch C11865-1 (Castleton OPR microfilm, source 1067953): James Telfer baptised 14 Jul 1761, parents **John Telfer & Elspeth Young**. This strengthens the entire line by providing a primary-source anchor one generation back.

**Ancestry/FindAGrave Caveat** — The FindAGrave James Telfer page's descriptive text about the 8 children may derive from the same genealogical research as the WikiTree entries, not from independent original records. However, the Statutory Death Index for William Telfer is an independent primary source that confirms the family unit.

**Assessment:** Accept James Telfer (1761–1845) and Betty Hutton (1774–1853) as Francis Telfer's parents. Mark "strong secondary evidence" in the tree. An OPR baptismal search on ScotlandsPeople would be the next step for gold-standard confirmation.

Hannah Baker was born on 28 August 1855 at **Peachy Belt, South Australia**, the second child of **[[William John Baker (1831–1919)]]** and **[[Sophia Baker (1829–1901)|Sophia March]]**. Her father had emigrated from Devon, England; her mother from Norfolk.

Hannah lived to 1948, outliving her husband William Humphrey (who died 1926) by 22 years.

Through Hannah, your family tree reaches back to **two distinct English counties**:

|---|---|---|

James Telfer was born in 1761 at Sorbietrees, in the parish of Castleton, Roxburghshire (the Liddesdale region of the Scottish Borders). He worked as a farmer, likely at the family lands of Sorbietrees and Blackburnfoot in the Castleton area.

He married Betty Hutton around 1795. Together they raised at least eight children in the Liddesdale valley, spanning from James (born 1796) to William (born 1811). The parish of Castleton, centred on the village of Newcastleton, sits in the borderlands between Scotland and England — a rugged farming region where the Telfer name has been recorded for centuries.

James never emigrated to Australia. He lived his entire life in the Scottish Borders and was buried at Old Castleton Cemetery in Newcastleton. His son Francis emigrated to South Australia in 1838 aboard the *Prince George*, settling first at Chain of Ponds and later at Clare. Francis brought the Telfer name to Australia, where it continues through the South Australian branch.

## Life Summary

James Telfer was the first child and eldest son of [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] and his first wife [[Martha Allen]]. Born at Honeysuckle Flat, South Australia on 18 October 1866, James was the first of four children from this marriage and carried his paternal grandfather's name.

In 1895, James—then living at Tantanoola—was listed in the *Border Watch* Almanac as a newspaper agent for the district, suggesting he operated a local agency for the Mount Gambier newspaper. The 1894 Tantanoola Show concert featured him as a performer, and Border Watch advertisements from 1898 and 1900 confirm his newspaper agency at Tantanoola.

He married [[Alma Sporer (1881–1965)]] on 24 October 1917 at the Lutheran Church, Mount Gambier — James was 49, Alma was 37. Their only child, Vida, was born on 8 March 1919. James became a prominent community figure in Glencoe West: he was appointed a Justice of the Peace in 1924, served as District Council Auditor (re-elected 1927), and acted as Secretary of the Glencoe District Hall in 1929.

He died on 28 August 1946 at Glencoe West, South Australia, aged 79. His obituary in The Advertiser (2 Sep 1946) and The Chronicle (5 Sep 1946) described him as the beloved husband of Alma and loving father of Vida.

## Life Summary

John Charles Dillon was born in Dublin, Ireland around 1827, the son of John Boswell Dillon. He emigrated to South Australia, likely in the 1850s, where he met and married Elizabeth Beattie Telfer.

The marriage took place on **18 December 1856** at the residence of Francis Telfer, Chain of Ponds, SA — an area in the Mount Lofty Ranges northeast of Adelaide. By 1860, John had lodged a caveat for land sections 648, 5517, and 5521 in the Hundred of Para Wirra, one of the earliest property transactions under South Australia's innovative Torrens Title system.

John and Elizabeth raised nine children at their Para Wirra property between 1858 and 1871. The strong "Telfer" naming pattern across four of their sons (James, Robert, Francis, Adam) reflects Elizabeth's Scottish heritage and the close-knit Telfer family network.

John outlived Elizabeth by ten years, passing away on 28 April 1906 at Tea Tree Gully, SA, at the age of 79. He was buried at Houghton Cemetery, adjacent to his wife's plot.

John Telfer was born around 1840–1841 in Roxburghshire, Scotland, the son of James Telfer (1796–1863) and Elizabeth Beattie. He emigrated to South Australia with his family sometime after 1842 (his youngest brother Adam was born in Scotland that year).

---

## Life Story

John Telfer was born in **Adelaide, South Australia** on **28 May 1847** — the eldest surviving son of Scottish immigrant [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)|Francis Telfer]] and his third wife Margaret Wright. He grew up on the family farm at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills.

On **22 September 1874**, he married **Caroline Amelia Masters** at the Baptist Chapel, Tarlee. The marriage was announced in the South Australian Register. Caroline had immigrated from England as a young child with her family aboard the *Templar* in 1845.

John and Caroline settled at **Willow Plains, near Clare**, where they farmed for **47 years**. They raised six sons:

1. [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] (1875–1954) — Great-grandfather
2. Ernest John Telfer (1878–1953)
3. William James Telfer (1880–?)
4. Albert George Telfer (1881–?)
5. Walter William Telfer (1884–1966)
6. Edwin Gilbert Telfer (1887–?)

John was described as a **prominent Clare resident** and was actively associated with every community move in the Willow Plains district. He was a **prominent member of the Methodist Church**, serving as **superintendent of the Sunday-school for about 30 years** (per both Advertiser and Chronicle obituaries).

### The Double Bereavement — 1929

In a remarkable and tragic turn, **John and Caroline died within hours of each other** in August 1929. John passed away on **23 August 1929** at age 82, and Caroline followed him **the next day**, 24 August 1929. The *Register News-Pictorial* ran a photo with the headline:

> "THE LATE MRS. JOHN TELFER, of Clare, who died within a few hours of her husband. Both were prominent Clare residents."

They were buried together at **Clare Cemetery**.

As the Advertiser obituary noted:
> "He was a resident of Willow Plains for 47 years. He was actively associated with every movement inaugurated for the wellbeing of the district, and was a prominent member of the Methodist Church and Sunday-school. Mr. Telfer held the position of superintendent of the Sunday-school for about 30 years."

On 31 July 1846, Joseph, his wife Sophia, and **seven of their children** arrived in the Colony of South Australia aboard the ship **Canton**. Their youngest, John Henry, was born in the colony the following year at Reed Beds.

The March family were **free settlers** — not convicts — part of the wave of English agricultural families who helped build South Australia's farming economy.

Joseph died on 30 October 1883 in Prospect, Adelaide, at age 86, and is buried at North Road Cemetery, Nailsworth.

## Life Summary

Margaret Wright was the **third wife** of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]. She married him in South Australia after the deaths of his first wife Jean Murray (d. 1839) and second wife Dinah Flavel.

She was the mother of:

Francis Telfer married three times — an unusual number that sometimes causes confusion in genealogical records:

2. **Dinah Flavel** — second wife in South Australia
3. **Margaret Wright** — third wife and mother of John and the younger children

Some trees simply list "Margaret Telfer" as Francis's wife without specifying which marriage, leading to contradictions between sources.

## Life Summary

Robert Telfer was born in 1803 in Castleton, Roxburghshire, the fifth child and third son of James Telfer and Betty Hutton. He was baptised on 25 April 1803 in the Church of Scotland at Castleton parish, the same Liddesdale valley where the Telfer family had lived for generations.

Unlike his younger brother Francis, who emigrated to South Australia in 1838, Robert remained in the Scottish Borders his entire life. He married Elizabeth "Betty" Oliver around 1828. The 1841 census shows the couple living in Castleton with their young family, alongside Robert's older brother John Telfer (64), Violet Telfer (25), and William Telfer (22) — likely extended family sharing a household.

By 1851, Robert (now aged 46) was living in Castleton with only his daughters Elizabeth (17) and John (11) still at home. His wife Betty is absent from the 1851 census household — she may have died between 1841 and 1851, though her death has not been traced.

Robert's death at age 74 was registered in 1878 in the Castleton district. The statutory death registration records his mother's maiden surname as Hutton, confirming his parentage.

**Great-grandchildren:** Levi, Zabella

---

## Life Summary

Shirley Edna Telfer (née Parker) was the matriarch of the Telfer family — wife of [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]] for over 50 years, and mother of six children. She spent her life on the family farm in the Ungarra/Tumby Bay region of South Australia's Eyre Peninsula.

Her parents were **William Henry Parker** and **Caroline Edna Lawrie**, who married on 29 March 1917 at Long Plains, South Australia. Caroline Edna was the daughter of Robert Dunlop Lawrie and Caroline Hosking, connecting Shirley to the **Lawrie family** — Scottish pioneers who emigrated from Ayrshire to South Australia in the 1850s and helped establish the Alma Church of Christ.

Shirley raised her family in a strong Christian home. The Church of Christ was central to the Telfer family's life — Murray served as an elder and secretary at both Ungarra and Tumby Bay Churches of Christ for decades, and Shirley was a steadfast partner in that faith journey.

She passed away peacefully at Tumby Bay Hospital on Thursday, 23 February 2017, aged 87. Her funeral was held at the Church of Christ, Tumby Bay, on Wednesday, 1 March 2017, followed by burial at Tumby Bay Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, the family requested donations to the Tumby Bay Hospital Auxiliary.

---

| Date | Event |

| ~1917 | Parents married at Long Plains, SA |

- **Funeral Notice** — *Centralian Advocate*, 25 February 2017: Funeral conducted at Church of Christ, Tumby Bay, 1 March 2017 at 11:00am. Cortege proceeded to Tumby Bay Cemetery. Donations to Tumby Bay Hospital Auxiliary.
- **Robert Dunlop Lawrie — probate notice** (Nov 1918): Administration of estate of Robert Dunlop Lawrie, farmer of Long Plains, SA. Bagot's Executor and Trustee Company. — via Trove

- **Alberta Grace Lawrie / Carslake — Biographical Dictionary of Coorow, Carnamah, Three Springs** — confirms Alberta Grace Lawrie born 4 Sep 1882 Long Plains SA, daughter of Robert Dunlop Lawrie & Caroline Hosking, married George Alfred Carslake 6 Sep 1904. [View](https://www.carnamah.com.au/bio/alberta-grace-lawrie) — accessed 23 May 2026

---

## Family Connections

- **Parker family:** [[William Henry Parker (1893–1968)]] (father, born Long Plains SA 1893) and Caroline Edna Lawrie (mother). Shirley had four siblings: Avis, Howard Lindsay, Sydney Hugh, and William Humphrey. The Parker line traces back to [[William Humphrey Parker (1850–1926)]] (1850–1926) and [[David Parker (1822–1888)]] (1822–1888), Scottish immigrants from Ayrshire who arrived in SA in 1852.
- **Lawrie family:** Her mother [[Caroline Edna Lawrie (1890–1957)]] profile needed (1890–1957) was the daughter of Robert Dunlop Lawrie and Caroline Hosking. Edna's sister was Alberta Grace "Gracie" Lawrie, whose grandson is **Graham Carslake** (author of the Lawrie family history).
- **Telfer connection:** Through her marriage to Murray John Telfer, she joined one of the pioneering farming families of the Ungarra district — the Telfers arrived on Eyre Peninsula around 1905.

## Life Summary

Sophia March was born in Aylsham, Norfolk, England in March 1829, the third child of **[[Joseph March (1797–1883)]]** and **Sophia Webster**.

On 31 July 1846, at age 17, she arrived in the Colony of South Australia with her parents and **seven siblings** aboard the ship **Canton**. Her father was an agricultural labourer seeking opportunity in the new colony.

She married **[[William John Baker (1831–1919)]]** on 9 March 1853 in Adelaide, at age 23. They settled in the Gawler Plains / Peachy Belt district and raised nine children.

Sophia died on 1 December 1901 in Hyde Park, Adelaide, at age 72, and is buried at West Terrace Cemetery.

---

## Family Origins — The March Line from Norfolk

The March family were from **Aylsham, Norfolk, England** — deep East Anglian farming country. Her father [[Joseph March (1797–1883)]] was born there in 1797. Grandfather Joseph March (abt 1767–1831) was also from Aylsham.

**The family sailed to South Australia on the *Canton*, arriving 31 Jul 1846.** This was part of the wave of English free settlers who helped build the young colony.

---

## Early Life

William John Baker was born on **14 Apr 1831** in Bickleigh, Devonshire, England, the son of **James Baker** and **Jane Baker**. His early years were spent in the Devonshire countryside.

At age **19**, he emigrated to South Australia aboard the **Stag** (678 tons, Captain John Baker), departing **Plymouth on 22 Feb 1850** and arriving **Port Adelaide on 11 June 1850**. The passenger list records him as "William Baker, 19, Mason, Devon" — confirming both his age (born ~1831, supporting the 1831 date over 1829) and his trade as a **mason** (stone worker/builder), not a baker.

---

## Life in South Australia

Upon arrival, his first job was helping build a church in Adelaide. When work stalled, he and a friend walked through the countryside seeking work, sleeping in barns and empty houses. He later joined the **first gold rushes to Victoria**.

He married **[[Sophia Baker (1829–1901)|Sophia Marsh]]** on **9 March 1853** in Adelaide, South Australia. Sophia had arrived in the colony on 31 July 1846 with her parents **[[Joseph March (1797–1883)]]** and **Sophia Webster** aboard the ship *Canton*.

William and Sophia took up land near **Virginia** on the Adelaide Plains, farming and working as a mason. To earn income while clearing land, he used a team of bullocks to cart goods to the Burra copper mines and return with copper ore. He purchased Sections 4102, 4095, and 4096 near Stebonheath Davoren Road.

They settled in the **Gawler Plains / Peachy Belt / Port Gawler** area and raised **nine children** — five sons and four daughters.

---

## Later Life & Death

William died on **3 June 1919** in Hyde Park, a suburb of Adelaide, at approximately age 88. He is buried at **West Terrace Cemetery**, Adelaide. His wife Sophia predeceased him, dying on 1 Dec 1901 aged 72. Both are in the same grave at West Terrace Cemetery.
